v.why: Without a direct 0->3 edge, removing edge 5 leaves only the path through node 1 (edge 4), so the cell loses much more capacity or connectivity (cf. exp 61, -28 pts on C10).
A residual 0->3 skip keeps a guaranteed input-to-output path, so dropping edge 5 is far less damaging.
With edge 4 already absent, removing edge 5 leaves at most the single 0->3 edge feeding the output, which collapses the cell's depth or disconnects it.
When edge 5 is missing, the output relies on a single path, so adding a residual 0->3 skip adds a lot of gradient flow and diversity (cf. exp 22, +16.5 on IN16).
Replacing a parameterized conv on 0->3 with a skip removes capacity, whereas replacing none or pooling only adds a residual (cf. exp 19, negative on all three datasets).
Swapping a weak 1x1 conv for an identity loses little capacity and improves optimization, unlike swapping out a 3x3 conv (exp 83-84 positive on all three datasets).
Replacing the strongest op, a 3x3 conv, with an identity removes the most useful computation, while replacing 1x1, pool or none costs little (exp 99 positive vs. 92/93 negative).
Adding a 3x3 conv where there was no edge adds a new path and capacity, while overwriting an existing skip or pool often disrupts a useful structure (exp 41-42 positive vs. 35-38 negative).
Filling an empty 1->3 edge with a conv adds a path, while replacing skip, 1x1 or pool trades away existing benefits (exp 71 vs. 72-74).
Turning an absent 2->3 edge into a 3x3 conv connects node 2 to the output and adds depth, a larger gain than upgrading an existing op (cf. exp 4, +45.7 on IN16).
